title: Decode String
summary: Given an encoded string, return its decoded string by repeating the substring inside the square brackets exactly k times, where k is a positive integer.
statement: Given an encoded string, return its decoded string by repeating the substring inside the square brackets exactly k times, where k is a positive integer. Ensure the input string is valid with no extra white spaces or malformed brackets. The original data does not contain any digits, and digits are only used for specifying the repeat counts. The length of the output will not exceed 10^5.
constraints: 1 <= s.length <= 30; only lowercase letters, digits, and square brackets.
The encoding is valid; every repeat count is in [1,300]. Digits are counts, never literal output.
The decoded output length is at most 100,000. Repetitions can nest and concatenate.
hints: A bracketed group has the same grammar as the whole string; recursion fits naturally.
Let one parser consume characters up to the matching closing bracket and return that decoded section.
Read all count digits, skip [, recursively parse the child, skip ], and append count copies. Append literal letters directly.
One shared cursor ensures each bracket belongs to one level. Join pieces after parsing, and include expanded output size when analyzing cost.
editorial: The parser handles either a literal letter or a count followed by a bracketed subexpression. Recursive calls stop before their closing bracket so the caller can consume it. Counts need decimal accumulation, and separate groups concatenate. The grammar bounds recursion depth by the short encoded input. If n is encoded length, L decoded length, and d nesting depth, O(n+dL) is a conservative time bound for repeated string materialization, with O(n+L) space.

tests.explanation: Decode each group, then concatenate: aaa + bcbc = aaabcbc.
First 2[c] becomes cc, so the outer group is acc repeated three times: accaccacc.
